title: Protecting a backup tackle: chips, slides and quick throws (and how to read it in your drill)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: it still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, last updated Oct 12) and no review files, and the original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session, and no tool to add it was available). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson is about Thursday's game: Carolina will start backups at left tackle, left guard and right tackle (Ikem Ekwonu on PUP, Damien Lewis ruled out Wednesday, rookie Monroe Freeling for the injured Taylor Moton), and how an offense hides weak blockers is the heart of the brief's Under 47.5.

The big idea: a pass rusher who beats his blocker in under 3 seconds wrecks a pass play. When a tackle is a backup or a rookie, the offense can't just hope; it sends help. Every helper is a player who isn't running a route, so the offense trades some of its passing threat for time. That trade is visible before and right after the snap, which makes it useful for your drill and for betting.

Diagram: white = offense, yellow = defense. Yellow-outlined squares are the backups (Carolina's LG and RT Thursday). Arrows 1–2 are the helpers, arrow 3 the line's slide, 4 the quarterback's quick drop. Numbers match the steps below.

  1. Tight end chip (1). The tight end lines up just outside the weak tackle. At the snap he hits the defensive end for a beat, knocking him off his path, then slips into a short route. The rusher loses half a second; the offense loses a deep receiver. You'll see it a lot from Carolina's tight ends on Freeling's side Thursday.
  2. Running back chip (2). The back starts beside the quarterback in the shotgun, steps up, punches the same rusher, then leaks to the flat as the quarterback's safety valve. That's why the brief leans "Chuba Hubbard: 15+ receiving yards": a pressured Bryce Young dumps it to his back (Hubbard has 15 of the 21 catches by Carolina running backs).
  3. Slide protection (3). The whole line shifts its assignments toward the weak side, so the guard next to the backup takes the inside rusher and the tackle only has to worry about the outside one. The cost: the other side is left with one-on-one blocks, which is where a smart defense then attacks (a stunt or a blitz from the far side).
  4. Quick throws (4). The simplest fix: a three-step drop and a throw in about 2.5 seconds, before the rush arrives: slants, hitches, quick outs, screens (Lesson 37). Young already faces pressure on 44.3% of drop-backs when defenses rush four or fewer, the NFL's highest rate, and Green Bay pressures on 38.5% without blitzing, 4th (Bettors Insider). Expect lots of short throws.
  5. Why this lowers scoring. Seven blockers mean three receivers; quick throws mean short gains. An offense playing this way needs 10–12 plays to score instead of a few big ones, and every extra play is another chance for a sack, a penalty or a stalled drive. That's the Under's football reason. The risk to it: the defense guesses wrong and a short throw breaks for a long gain (Tetairoa McMillan is the Carolina player who can do that).
  6. The defense's answers. Rush the weak tackle with a stunt (two linemen crossing), overload the side the line didn't slide to, or drop extra defenders into coverage, since only three receivers are out. Green Bay is short its own pieces (Devonte Wyatt questionable, Micah Parsons out), so watch whether it blitzes or trusts four rushers.

How to log it in your drill: on 2nd- or 3rd-and-long, a tight end lined up tight next to a tackle and a back beside the quarterback in the shotgun usually means PASS with extra protection, not a run, even though it looks "heavy." The tell after the snap: the tight end and back stay home (or chip, then release late) while three receivers run. The same tight-end-in-tight look on 1st-and-10 or short yardage, with the quarterback under center, leans RUN (Lesson 1: personnel plus down and distance). When the drill scores a chip-and-release play, it's a pass.

Real examples to watch: Thursday, Panthers at Packers (Fri 9:15 a.m. JST / Thu 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime Video): Carolina's right side, where Freeling faces Green Bay's edge rushers. Sunday night, Eagles at Commanders (Mon 10:20 a.m. JST / Sun 5:20 p.m. PT, NBC): Philadelphia without RT Lane Johnson. Monday night, Bears at Seahawks (Tue 10:15 a.m. JST / Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN): Seattle with LT Charles Cross doubtful. In college, Ohio State at USC (Sun 8:30 a.m. JST / Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, NBC).

Video: search YouTube for "chip block explained NFL," "slide protection vs man protection," and "quick game three step drop explained."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 7: Read the snap)

quiz.q: Carolina's rookie right tackle faces a fast edge rusher. What is a "chip"?
o: A tight end or back hits the rusher for a moment, then runs a route
A snap before the defense is set
quiz.w: A chip is a one-beat block that knocks the rusher off his path; then the helper releases as a short receiver.

quiz.q: If both the tight end and the running back stay in to block, how many players are running routes right away?
quiz.w: 5 linemen + TE + RB = 7 blockers. With the quarterback, that's 8 of 11, leaving 3 receivers.

quiz.q: Why do offenses protecting backup tackles often score less?
o: More blockers and quick throws mean fewer deep shots, so drives need more plays and stall more
Referees only call holding on rookies
They have to run on every 3rd down
quiz.w: Three receivers and short throws mean 10 to 12 plays per scoring drive, with more chances for a sack, penalty or stall. That's the football behind Thursday's Under.

quiz.q: Drill: 3rd-and-8, shotgun, tight end lined up next to the right tackle, running back beside the quarterback. Your call?
o: RUN, because the tight end is in tight
PASS: it's long yardage, and the TE and RB are likely extra protection
Can't tell anything before the snap
quiz.w: Down and distance comes first. On 3rd-and-long, a tight end in tight and a back beside the QB usually mean a protected pass; watch them stay home or chip and release.
